difficultyReason: The argument involves two moves — establishing a general principle about diagnostic accuracy, then applying it to reject an opposing position. Test-takers must distinguish the full two-step technique from answers that capture only one step or describe a different operation.
stimulus: Physician: My colleague argues that imaging results alone are sufficient to diagnose a particular nerve disorder. But imaging can only detect structural abnormalities, and the disorder in question sometimes produces no structural changes whatsoever. Any diagnostic method that can fail to detect a condition even when that condition is fully present is not sufficient on its own. Therefore, my colleague's view cannot be correct.

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing experimental data to establish that a widely used diagnostic tool produces unreliable results

choices.label: B
choices.text: applying a general principle about diagnostic sufficiency to show that a specific claim is mistaken

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two different medical conditions to undermine a colleague's recommendation

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring a causal relationship between a structural abnormality and a nerve disorder from observed correlations

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to expert consensus in order to cast doubt on an alternative diagnostic approach

explanations.correct: The physician states a general principle (a method that can miss a fully present condition is insufficient on its own), then applies it directly to imaging for this disorder, concluding that the colleague's claim fails. That is exactly applying a general principle to reject a specific claim.
explanations.A: No experimental data are cited; the physician argues from the nature of imaging and a stated principle. This answer invents evidence not in the argument.
explanations.C: No analogy between two conditions is drawn; the argument concerns one condition and one method. This is an 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.D: No correlation is observed and no causal inference is made; causation is never the subject. This is a content-over-technique trap.
explanations.E: No expert consensus is invoked; the physician relies on a principled definition, not authority. This is an extreme-verb / wrong-move trap.

difficultyReason: The argument sets up a rival position and then defeats it by producing a counterexample. Students must track whether the argument is generalizing, analogizing, or counterexampling — three superficially similar moves — and select the one that correctly describes the structure.
stimulus: Historian: Some scholars maintain that economic hardship is always the primary driver of revolutionary movements. Yet the French Revolution of 1789 erupted during a period of relative economic growth in several regions of France, with revolutionary ferment strongest among literate professionals who were not themselves impoverished. This case alone demonstrates that the scholars' universal claim cannot stand.
questionStem: The historian's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: surveys a broad range of historical cases to support a statistical generalization about revolutions

choices.label: B
choices.text: appeals to an authority on revolutionary history to cast doubt on a competing interpretation

choices.label: C
choices.text: cites a specific historical instance as a counterexample to a universal claim

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws an analogy between the French Revolution and a contemporary political movement

choices.label: E
choices.text: infers that economic conditions are irrelevant to revolutionary movements based on a single case

explanations.correct: The historian identifies a universal claim (economic hardship is always the primary driver) and then produces the French Revolution as a case that violates it, which is precisely the move of citing a counterexample to a universal claim.
explanations.A: Only one case is used, not a broad survey. This is the mis-scaled trap — describing the argument as a generalization when it is a specific refutation.
explanations.B: No authority is cited; the historian relies on historical facts, not another scholar's endorsement.
explanations.D: No contemporary movement appears; the argument is confined to one historical episode.
explanations.E: The conclusion is that the universal claim fails, not that economics is wholly irrelevant — this overstates the argument's conclusion (extreme-verb trap).

difficultyReason: The argument uses an analogy between two economic situations — one with observable data and one without — mirroring the structure of the authentic anchor. Test-takers must recognize the analogical move and resist traps describing causal inference or statistical generalization.
stimulus: Economist: We have detailed productivity data for the manufacturing sector following last year's regulatory overhaul, and those data show a marked decline in output per worker. We have no comparably direct data for the agricultural sector, which underwent the same overhaul at the same time. Given the structural similarities between the two sectors' labor arrangements, we can reasonably conclude that agricultural productivity per worker also declined.
questionStem: The economist's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: uses data from one sector where measurement is possible to draw a conclusion about an analogous sector where direct measurement is unavailable

choices.label: B
choices.text: establishes a causal connection between regulatory policy and productivity by comparing outcomes across multiple industries

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers a general economic principle from observed trends in a single industry

choices.label: D
choices.text: predicts future productivity levels by extrapolating from historical baseline data

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejects a competing economic model by identifying an internal inconsistency in its assumptions

explanations.correct: The economist has direct productivity data for manufacturing, lacks direct data for agriculture, notes structural similarity, and infers the same outcome. This is exactly the pattern of using an observable case to draw a conclusion about an analogous unobservable case.
explanations.B: No causal connection is established; the argument infers an outcome by analogy, not by demonstrating causation. 'Establishes' is also an extreme verb the argument does not warrant.
explanations.C: The movement is in the opposite direction — from one sector to another, not from a sector to a general principle.
explanations.D: The conclusion concerns the same regulatory overhaul period, not a future event. This is the mis-temporal trap.
explanations.E: No competing model is identified or attacked; the argument is constructive, not adversarial.

difficultyReason: The argument appeals to a definition to settle a disputed classification. Students must identify the definitional move rather than confusing it with an empirical or analogical argument, and must distinguish the correct answer from a trap that accurately describes only half of the reasoning.
stimulus: Legal scholar: Critics argue that the new surveillance ordinance constitutes an unlawful search. However, an unlawful search, by legal definition, requires an intrusion into a space in which the subject has a reasonable expectation of privacy. The ordinance in question covers only activity conducted in publicly visible areas, where no such expectation exists. The critics' objection therefore fails on its own terms.
questionStem: The legal scholar's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing precedent established by prior court decisions to override the critics' interpretation of the ordinance

choices.label: B
choices.text: appealing to the accepted definition of a legal concept to show that a particular case does not fall within it

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between the new ordinance and a prior surveillance law that courts have upheld

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrating that the critics' position leads to a conclusion that is inconsistent with their own stated values

choices.label: E
choices.text: surveying empirical evidence about privacy expectations to refute the critics' factual claim

explanations.correct: The scholar invokes the accepted legal definition of 'unlawful search' (requires intrusion into a space with a reasonable privacy expectation), then shows the ordinance targets only public spaces lacking that expectation — a definitional exclusion of the case from the category.
explanations.A: No court precedent is cited; the argument rests on a definitional standard, not judicial authority.
explanations.C: No prior law or analogous ordinance is introduced; the argument stays within the current ordinance and the definition.
explanations.D: The critics' values are not mentioned; the inconsistency alleged is between their objection and the legal definition, not their personal commitments. This is the 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.E: No empirical survey of privacy expectations is conducted; the claim that public spaces lack such expectations is treated as a definitional given.

difficultyReason: The argument rejects an opposing position by deriving an absurd consequence from it. Test-takers must recognize reductio ad absurdum and distinguish it from counterexample reasoning and from causal-inference traps.
stimulus: Ethicist: Some philosophers contend that an action is morally obligatory whenever it would produce a net increase in overall happiness. But if that were true, then a surgeon would be morally required to harvest the organs of one healthy patient to save five dying ones, since doing so would increase net happiness. Because virtually everyone recognizes that such an act would be deeply wrong, the proposed criterion cannot be correct.
questionStem: The ethicist's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: appeals to empirical research on human moral intuitions to establish a competing ethical theory

choices.label: B
choices.text: cites a generally recognized moral judgment to undermine a criterion that would entail a conflicting conclusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes from a single thought experiment to a broad conclusion about the nature of moral obligation

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws an analogy between medical ethics and philosophical ethics to resolve a conceptual dispute

choices.label: E
choices.text: identifies a logical contradiction within the philosophical criterion by analyzing its internal assumptions

explanations.correct: The ethicist takes the opposing criterion, derives from it a consequence (organ harvesting is obligatory) that virtually everyone recognizes as morally wrong, and uses that widely accepted moral judgment to reject the criterion. This is citing a generally recognized judgment to undermine a criterion that entails a conflicting conclusion.
explanations.A: No empirical research is cited; the ethicist relies on a widely shared intuition, not a study. And no competing theory is established — only the rival criterion is rejected.
explanations.C: The argument rejects a criterion rather than building a generalization; the thought experiment is the vehicle of refutation, not the basis of a new general claim.
explanations.D: The argument does not compare two domains — medical ethics and philosophical ethics — as analogous fields; the medical scenario is a logical test case for one criterion.
explanations.E: The criterion is not internally contradictory; the problem is that it generates an externally unacceptable conclusion, not that its own assumptions conflict.

difficultyReason: The argument uses elimination — ruling out all alternatives to establish the remaining option. Students must recognize this structure and not confuse it with analogy, authority appeal, or causal inference, all of which appear as tempting traps.
stimulus: Environmental scientist: The sharp decline in the local amphibian population must be attributable to the increase in ultraviolet radiation reaching the lake bottom. Habitat loss is not a factor, since the wetland area has actually expanded over the same period. Introduced predators have been ruled out by recent wildlife surveys. Disease has been excluded by comprehensive pathological testing. UV radiation is the only remaining candidate.
questionStem: The environmental scientist's argument derives its conclusion by

choices.label: A
choices.text: drawing an analogy between the local lake ecosystem and a comparable ecosystem in which UV radiation caused a similar decline

choices.label: B
choices.text: citing the results of controlled laboratory experiments that demonstrate the harmful effects of UV radiation on amphibians

choices.label: C
choices.text: systematically eliminating alternative explanations to establish the only remaining candidate as the cause

choices.label: D
choices.text: identifying a correlation between UV radiation levels and amphibian population counts across multiple study sites

choices.label: E
choices.text: applying a general ecological principle about the sensitivity of amphibians to radiation to this particular case

explanations.correct: The scientist goes through habitat loss, predators, and disease one by one, dismissing each, and concludes that UV radiation must be the cause because it is all that remains. This is argument by elimination.
explanations.A: No comparable ecosystem is introduced; the argument stays within the local lake. This is the 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.B: No laboratory experiments are cited; the evidence cited concerns field surveys and pathological tests, not controlled lab work.
explanations.D: No cross-site correlation data are mentioned; the argument is purely eliminative, not correlational.
explanations.E: No general ecological principle about amphibian radiation sensitivity is stated; the argument proceeds by elimination, not by applying a stored principle.

difficultyReason: The argument infers from a sample to a population. Students must recognize this inductive move and distinguish it from analogical reasoning, definitional appeal, and causal inference — all present as traps — while noticing that the 'partially true' trap describes one premise rather than the full reasoning move.
stimulus: Sociologist: A recent longitudinal study tracked eight hundred randomly selected adults across fifteen cities over a ten-year period. Researchers found that, within this group, individuals who reported consistent daily exercise routines had significantly lower rates of clinical depression than those who did not. We can therefore conclude that, among adults generally, regular exercise is associated with reduced rates of clinical depression.

choices.label: A
choices.text: establishing a causal mechanism by which exercise chemically reduces the neurological basis of depression

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogy between the study participants and a different population whose mental health outcomes are already known

choices.label: C
choices.text: appealing to expert consensus among psychiatrists about the therapeutic benefits of physical activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring a general population-level association from observed patterns in a representative sample

choices.label: E
choices.text: applying an established psychological principle to account for the depression rates observed in the study

explanations.correct: The sociologist observes a pattern in a sample (800 randomly selected adults) and extends that pattern to the general adult population. This is the classic sample-to-population inductive move.
explanations.A: No causal mechanism is identified; the conclusion explicitly uses 'associated with,' not 'causes.' Claiming a causal mechanism is established overstates what the argument does (extreme-verb trap).
explanations.B: No second population is introduced; the argument moves from the sample directly to the general adult population, not via analogy with another known group.
explanations.C: No expert consensus is invoked; the argument relies solely on the study's data.
explanations.E: No pre-existing psychological principle is applied; the argument builds up from data rather than applying a stored principle downward.

difficultyReason: The argument rejects a technological claim by showing it is inconsistent with a broadly accepted principle about how verification works. Students must distinguish this from counterexample reasoning, authority appeals, and causal arguments — all present as traps.
stimulus: Software engineer: Proponents of this new encryption protocol claim it is unbreakable. Yet any claim that a system is unbreakable requires that every possible attack method has been considered and shown to fail. No finite team of engineers can enumerate every conceivable attack vector on a sufficiently complex system. Therefore, the claim that this protocol is unbreakable cannot be justified.
questionStem: The software engineer's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: identifies a specific attack vector that the protocol's designers failed to consider, thereby disproving the protocol's security

choices.label: B
choices.text: appeals to a general epistemic principle about what is required for a claim of completeness to show that a specific security claim is unjustified

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws an analogy between the new encryption protocol and a prior protocol that was eventually compromised

choices.label: D
choices.text: surveys the opinions of cryptography experts to establish that the protocol has not been independently verified

choices.label: E
choices.text: infers from the complexity of the protocol that it is likely to contain undiscovered flaws

explanations.correct: The engineer states a general epistemic principle (claiming unbreakability requires showing every attack method fails), then applies it: since no team can enumerate all attack vectors, the claim cannot be justified. This is applying a general principle about what justification requires to show a specific claim falls short.
explanations.A: No specific attack vector is identified; the argument is about the impossibility of complete enumeration, not about a particular overlooked attack. This invents a move the argument does not make.
explanations.C: No prior protocol is mentioned; the argument is entirely about the logical requirements for the current claim.
explanations.D: No expert survey is cited; the engineer's objection is principled, not empirical.
explanations.E: The argument's conclusion is about justifiability of the claim, not about the likelihood of flaws — a subtle but important content-over-technique distinction.

difficultyReason: The argument involves a linguist setting up a competing claim and then using a specific observable phenomenon to challenge it. The correct answer must capture both the adversarial setup and the evidential move; traps either drop the adversarial component or misdescribe the evidence as a generalization.
stimulus: Linguist: Some cognitive scientists assert that all human languages share a universal deep grammar encoded in our biology. However, recent fieldwork on Pirahã, a language spoken by an Amazonian community, has documented the absence of grammatical features — such as recursion — that these scientists consider universal and innate. If even one language lacks a supposedly universal feature, the universality claim is refuted.
questionStem: The linguist's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: generalizes from patterns observed in a single language to a conclusion about the structure of all human languages

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws an analogy between Pirahã grammar and the grammatical systems of other Amazonian languages

choices.label: C
choices.text: uses a specific documented case to challenge a claim that a grammatical feature is universal to all human languages

choices.label: D
choices.text: appeals to the authority of fieldwork researchers to override the theoretical conclusions of cognitive scientists

choices.label: E
choices.text: argues that biological innateness cannot be the source of any grammatical feature because languages differ from one another

explanations.correct: The linguist identifies a universal claim (all languages share certain innate grammatical features) and uses Pirahã as a documented case lacking those features — a counterexample — to refute the universal claim. The answer accurately describes this as using a specific documented case to challenge a universality claim.
explanations.A: The argument moves in the opposite direction: from Pirahã as a case to the rejection of a universal claim, not from Pirahã to a new generalization about all languages. This is the mis-scaled trap.
explanations.B: No other Amazonian languages are introduced; Pirahã is used alone as a counterexample.
explanations.D: The argument does not pit researchers' authority against scientists' authority; it uses documented empirical findings as evidence, not as an appeal to credibility.
explanations.E: The conclusion is narrower — that this specific universality claim fails — not the sweeping claim that innateness can explain no grammatical feature.

difficultyReason: The argument proceeds by drawing an analogy between two arts-funding situations — one with outcome data and one without — to support a conclusion about the second. Students must isolate the analogical structure and resist traps that describe causal inference, generalization, or definitional appeal.
stimulus: Arts administrator: Last year, the city provided direct subsidies to twelve independent theater companies, and surveys showed that attendance at subsidized venues increased by thirty percent while overall attendance in the broader theater market stayed flat. This year, the city is considering identical subsidies for independent music ensembles. Because the market conditions and audience demographics for independent music are closely comparable to those for independent theater, we should expect a similar attendance boost for the music ensembles.
questionStem: The arts administrator's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers a causal relationship between public subsidies and increased attendance by comparing subsidized and unsubsidized venues in the same market

choices.label: B
choices.text: applies a general economic principle about arts funding to predict outcomes in a specific municipal context

choices.label: C
choices.text: uses observed outcomes in one arts sector to draw a conclusion about expected outcomes in a comparable arts sector

choices.label: D
choices.text: surveys a broad range of arts subsidy programs to establish a statistical pattern linking funding to attendance growth

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejects the city's prior funding model by showing that the data from theater subsidies contradict its underlying assumptions

explanations.correct: The administrator has outcome data from one sector (theater), notes comparable conditions in another sector (music), and concludes the same outcome should be expected there. This is the analogical move of using results in one observable case to draw a conclusion about a comparable case.
explanations.A: While the argument does rely on the subsidy-attendance relationship, it does not establish causation — it infers by analogy that the same pattern will hold in a new sector. Saying it 'infers a causal relationship' misdescribes the reasoning move (content-over-technique trap).
explanations.B: No general economic principle is invoked; the administrator draws directly on the theater case without appealing to a stored principle.
explanations.D: Only one prior program (theater) is referenced, not a broad survey of many programs. This is the mis-scaled trap.
explanations.E: The administrator supports the subsidy model, not rejects it; the theater data are used constructively. This describes a different, adversarial argument.
